title: Néel-Vector-Dependent Altermagnetic Spin Splitting in the One-Dimensional Limit
abstract: Altermagnetism is normally identified by nonrelativistic spin-split bands in a compensated collinear magnet. Under one-dimensional confinement, however, this diagnostic can disappear: a boundary-compatible sublattice-exchange operation may leave the only Bloch momentum unchanged, forcing the nonrelativistic spin-up and spin-down spectra to coincide. We show that nonrelativistic spin degeneracy can coexist with relativistic spin splitting in a compensated one-dimensional magnet. In a Lieb-based construction, confinement along the diagonal cancels the projected $d$-wave spin splitting while preserving the real-space sublattice-exchange motif. Spin-orbit coupling (SOC) then locks spin to the lattice, so the Néel-vector orientation selects a magnetic line group that can reveal spin-split bands. Using fully compensated $[110]$ Ta$_2$TeSeO nanoribbons as a prototype, we find spin-degenerate nonrelativistic bands and sizable SOC splitting in the inherited easy-axis domain, $\mathbf N\parallel[100]$ or $[010]$. For sufficiently wide ribbons that retain the parent easy-axis order, this splitting is an equilibrium property. The easy-axis ribbon also supports a right-moving-mode spin polarization of about $35\%$ at finite ideal conductance. Our results establish one-dimensional fully compensated altermagnetic functionality hidden inside apparently conventional antiferromagnetic bands.
summary: This work explores how altermagnetism, typically identified by spin-split bands, can hide in one-dimensional magnetic nanoribbons due to geometric confinement. By incorporating Spin-Orbit Coupling (SOC), the authors demonstrate that a robust, SOC-driven spin splitting can reappear, establishing a mechanism for 1D altermagnetism hidden within seemingly conventional antiferromagnetic materials.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the diagnostic signature of altermagnetism (spin-split bands in nonrelativistic spectra) can disappear under one-dimensional (1D) confinement, and how relativistic spin splitting can reappear despite this nonrelativistic degeneracy.
main_result: The study shows that 1D fully compensated altermagnetic functionality can exist, characterized by spin-degenerate nonrelativistic bands but sizable SOC-induced spin splitting when the Néel vector is oriented along specific crystal directions.
method: The research uses first-principles Wannier Hamiltonians with spin matrices to model the electronic structure and analyze the effect of symmetry operations on spin splitting.
model_or_system: The system studied is fully compensated [110] Ta2TeSeO nanoribbons, modeled using a Lieb-based construction, which is analyzed in the 1D limit.
key_observables: Spin expectation value along the Néel vector ($\sigma \cdot \hat{N}$), SOC-induced spin splitting, and right-moving-mode spin polarization ($P_{	ext{mode},q}$).
important_parameters: One-dimensional confinement, Néel-vector orientation ($\mathbf{N}$), and the presence/absence of Spin-Orbit Coupling (SOC).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ribbon is wide enough to retain the parent easy-axis magnetic order, and transport calculations rely on ideal Landauer conductance models.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dimensional reduction process, the spin-degenerate non-SOC bands, and the emergence of spin-split relativistic spectra for various Néel vector orientations, alongside mode polarization plots.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical problem of 1D confinement suppressing the altermagnetic signature, then uses a Lieb-based model to calculate the electronic structure, demonstrating the SOC-induced splitting, and finally analyzes the resulting spin polarization in transport measurements.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the concept of symmetry-protected topological phases and the interplay between lattice confinement and relativistic quantum effects (SOC) is relevant to understanding engineered quantum materials.
